title: Sell Mineral Rights in Culberson County, TX/NM
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Culberson County, TX | Royalty Buyer
metaDescription: Culberson County minerals sit in one of the deepest, richest parts of the Delaware Basin. Get a straight cash-offer conversation from a retired engineer.
heroLead: Culberson County is remote even by West Texas standards, but the rock underneath it is some of the thickest, most stacked pay in the entire Delaware Basin.
intro: I spent years working completions on Delaware Basin wells where the target zones sat deeper and the pressures ran higher than almost anywhere else in the Permian, and Culberson County was one of the counties where that showed up most clearly on the logs. The Bone Spring and Wolfcamp intervals here are thick enough that a single section can support multiple stacked landing zones, which is part of why big operators moved in aggressively over the last decade.

That intensity of development is good news if you own minerals or royalty in Culberson County, because it usually means more wells competing for the same acreage over time. It also means the interest can be genuinely complicated to value correctly, which is where I can help before you sign anything.

sections.heading: A basin that got serious attention late
paragraphs: Culberson County didn't see meaningful horizontal drilling until well after Reeves and Loving counties to the north were already established, largely because the geology here runs deeper and the completions were more expensive to justify. Once operators proved the economics, though, Culberson became one of the more heavily permitted counties in the Delaware, with large public E&Ps building multi-well pad programs across big blocks of acreage.

That later start actually works in a mineral owner's favor in one specific way: much of the acreage here was leased and developed under more modern lease terms, with better royalty fractions and clearer Pugh clause language than you'd find on a lease signed in the 1970s. If your family's lease dates back further than that, it's still worth having me look at it, because older leases sometimes carry provisions that affect what a buyer will pay.

sections.heading: What makes an offer higher or lower here
paragraphs: The biggest swing factor in Culberson County is how close your tract sits to the core development areas where multiple operators have already drilled and permitted stacked laterals. Acreage in the thick of that activity carries a different risk profile than acreage on the fringe where development is speculative, and I price accordingly rather than quoting one flat number for the whole county.

Decline stage matters too. A Wolfcamp well two years into production behaves very differently than one ten years in, and since Culberson's horizontal history is relatively young, a lot of the interests I see here are still on steep early decline curves. That's not a bad thing for value, it just means the numbers move faster than they would on an older, flatter-producing well, so I always want a recent check stub to see where the curve currently sits.

sections.heading: Ownership realities in this part of the Delaware
paragraphs: A fair amount of Culberson County mineral ownership traces to large historic ranch holdings, sometimes with minerals split among an extended family or held inside a trust that was never fully wound down. If your interest comes through a trust or an estate that's still in some stage of probate, that doesn't stop me from making an offer, but it does affect the title work and the closing timeline.

I also regularly buy small non-operated working interests here, usually inherited alongside a royalty share. Working interest owners carry a portion of the drilling and operating costs, which is a very different risk than pure royalty, so if you're not sure which kind of interest you hold, send me the division order and I'll tell you plainly what you're looking at.

sections.heading: Getting a real number, not a form-letter estimate
paragraphs: I don't send blind mailers quoting a per-acre number for Culberson County, because the range between a fringe undeveloped tract and a core-acreage producing interest is too wide for that to mean anything. Send me your division order, a recent check stub, or even just the section, block, and abstract number, and I'll pull what's publicly available and build a range specific to your interest.

This isn't tax or legal advice, and for questions about how a sale affects your estate or your tax return, talk to your CPA or attorney. What I offer is a candid conversation and a written offer with no obligation to move forward, and no pressure if the number isn't right for you.

faqs.question: Is Culberson County still an active area for new drilling?
faqs.answer: Yes. It remains one of the more actively permitted counties in the Delaware Basin, with several large operators running multi-well pad development across stacked Wolfcamp and Bone Spring zones. That ongoing activity is a meaningful factor in how I value undeveloped or lightly developed acreage here.

faqs.question: My family's minerals are held in a trust, can you still buy the interest?
faqs.answer: Generally yes. Trust-held interests just require the trustee to sign, and I'll ask for the trust documents to confirm who has authority. It adds a step to closing but doesn't prevent a sale.

faqs.question: Why would an offer on an undeveloped Culberson County tract be lower than a producing one?
faqs.answer: An undeveloped tract has no current cash flow, so its value depends on the likelihood and timing of a future well. A producing interest has a visible decline curve I can analyze directly, which generally supports a stronger offer relative to a speculative tract.

faqs.question: Do you buy small fractional royalty interests in Culberson County?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's common here given how much acreage is split among heirs of larger historic ranch holdings. A small decimal interest under active development can still be worth a real offer.
